title: Epiplexity Guided Data Selection and Generation for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: A learning-progress signal, the area under the loss curve, can be maximized online to steer both data selection and data generation toward transferable data.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; concept plots, then two feedback-loop diagrams
description: Three panels share one orange 'epiplexity signal' color. Panel (a) stacks three small loss-curve plots labeled Trivial, Structured and Noise. The area between each curve and its final loss is shaded orange. Only the Structured curve has a large area. Beside each plot is a small ID/OOD bar chart, and only Structured has high OOD performance. Panel (b) shows four domain boxes (Wikipedia, ArXiv, GitHub, PubMed) feeding a Learner box through arrows of varying thickness. The Learner connects to a Scaling-law box. An orange feedback arrow returns from the scaling-law box to the domains, labeled π_k. Panel (c) shows a Generator box emitting data X_t to a Learner. The data also goes to a dashed Buffer. A pre/post loss bar pair gives a reward r_t, and an orange arrow carries the reward back to the Generator.
caption: Epiplexity for data selection and generation. (a) Epiplexity, S(t), can be estimated as the area between the learner’s training loss curve and its final loss as a function of training tokens. Data which is trivial to learn or unlearnable will yield low estimates of epiplexity and result in lower performance in OOD downstream tasks. (b) For data selection, we use scaling laws to forecast the per-domain loss curves and predict the change in epiplexity, ∂ˆS(t)/∂nj, as a function of in-domain tokens. We then greedily maximize ∂ˆS(t)/∂nj to determine the sampling weights πk used in adaptive reweighting of the domains during data selection. (c) For data generation, we estimate d ˆS(t)/dt as the learner’s loss reduction over an evaluation buffer B, which stores the past training data. We set d ˆS(t)/dt as the reward and update the generator via REINFORCE to steer the generator toward producing epiplexity-maximizing synthetic data.
abstract: Modern systems are increasingly expected to transfer across tasks not specified during training. What data facilitates generalization to unanticipated settings? One hypothesis is that data with more structural information could contain shared circuits and subprograms that may be recycled in a wider array of downstream settings. Epiplexity, a recently proposed measure of the structural information a compute-bounded learner can extract from data, offers a mechanism to reason about this relationship. As existing estimators for epiplexity only operate on data already seen during training, we show how to operationalize epiplexity as an online training signal by greedily maximizing its stepwise gain in two settings. For data selection, we fit scaling laws to the training loss curves of natural data domains to predict the expected epiplexity gain as a function of training tokens, and use this signal to adaptively determine the sampling weights over domains during training. For synthetic data generation, where no domain structure exists, we reward a generator with the change in epiplexity of a learner's synthetic training data and use REINFORCE policy gradients to guide the generator toward an epiplexity-maximizing distribution. In both cases, we find higher epiplexity predicts improved downstream performance on zero-shot and fine-tuning tasks, supporting the hypothesis that data rich in structural information yield representations that better transfer across domains.
